passages.happening:
After the laments over Babylon, John hears heaven: “After this I heard a sound like the roar of a great multitude in heaven, shouting: ‘Hallelujah! Salvation and glory and power belong to our God! For His judgments are true and just. He has judged the great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her immorality. He has avenged the blood of His servants that was poured out by her hand’” (verses 1-2).

“And a second time they called out: ‘Hallelujah! Her smoke rises forever and ever’” (verse 3).

The twenty-four elders and the four living creatures fall down and worship God who sits on the throne, saying, “Amen, Hallelujah!” (verse 4). Then a voice comes from the throne: “Praise our God, all you who serve Him, and those who fear Him, small and great alike!” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The laments of chapter 18 came from those who loved Babylon. Now the answer comes from heaven. Kings and merchants mourned what they had lost. Heaven praises God for what he has done.

‘Hallelujah’ is a Hebrew word meaning ‘praise the LORD’. It joins the verb ‘to praise’ to Yah, a short form of God's covenant name. It is common in the Psalms, and these verses are the only place it appears in the New Testament. It comes four times here, like choirs answering one another in a temple. The church's praise at the end is Israel's praise from the Psalms.

Listen to what they praise. Not destruction for its own sake. They praise God because ‘His judgments are true and just’, the words the altar spoke in 16:7. They praise him because ‘He has avenged the blood of His servants’. The martyrs under the altar asked, ‘How long, O Lord ... until You avenge our blood?’ (6:10). This is the answer to that prayer.

‘Her smoke rises forever and ever.’ The words come from Isaiah's picture of Edom's ruin, a ruin that is never undone. Babylon will never rise again.

Then the voice from the throne calls everyone to praise, ‘small and great alike’. In heaven the famous and the unknown worship side by side. Rank no longer matters.
passages.ot:
The Hallelujah comes from the Psalms: “Hallelujah! Give praise, O servants of the LORD; praise the name of the LORD” (Psalm 113:1), and “Hallelujah! Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever” (Psalm 106:1).

The rising smoke is Isaiah's word over Edom: “Its smoke will ascend forever. From generation to generation it will lie desolate” (Isaiah 34:10).
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that heaven's first word after Babylon falls is praise to God, not delight in her pain. Ask which prayers of your own for justice you would want to see answered like this. And ask whether you can join the praise of ‘small and great alike’ without needing to be among the great.

passages.happening:
John hears “a sound like the roar of a great multitude, like the rushing of many waters, and like a mighty rumbling of thunder, crying out: ‘Hallelujah! For the Lord our God the Almighty reigns’” (verse 6).

“Let us rejoice and be glad and give Him the glory. For the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready. She was given clothing of fine linen, bright and pure.” John adds: “For the fine linen she wears is the righteous acts of the saints” (verses 7-8).

The angel tells John to write a saying about “those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.” And he says, “These are the true words of God” (verse 9).

“So I fell at his feet to worship him. But he told me, ‘Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you and your brothers who rely on the testimony of Jesus. Worship God! For the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy’” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
‘The Lord our God the Almighty reigns.’ The word for Almighty, pantokratōr, means ruler of all. The Greek Old Testament used it for ‘the LORD of hosts’. Revelation uses it nine times, in a world where Caesar seemed to hold all power. This line, with 11:15 and 19:16, is among the texts Handel set in the Hallelujah chorus of Messiah in 1742.

Then the great surprise: a wedding. The Old Testament pictured God as Israel's husband, and the New Testament speaks of Christ and the church in the same way. A wedding in Israel had two stages: a binding betrothal, and then, later, the bridegroom's coming to take his bride home, with a feast that could last for days. The church has been betrothed. Now the bridegroom comes.

The story that began with a man and a woman in a garden ends with a wedding between Christ and his people. Babylon was dressed in purple and scarlet, the costliest dyes, bought with others' lives. The bride is dressed in plain fine linen, ‘bright and pure’.

And notice how she gets it. She ‘was given’ it. And it is ‘the righteous acts of the saints’. Both are true. The bride's clothing is a gift, and it is also the life she has lived in response. Grace and faithfulness belong together.

Then John does something strange. He falls at the angel's feet to worship. The angel stops him at once: “Do not do that!” and “Worship God!” An angel, however glorious, is a fellow servant. Only God is to be worshipped. That makes it all the more striking that in this book the Lamb is worshipped with God (5:13). The angel refuses worship. The Lamb receives it.

‘The testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.’ True prophecy is witness to Jesus. That is what this whole book is.
passages.ot:
God as Israel's husband is the prophets' picture: “For your husband is your Maker— the LORD of Hosts is His name” (Isaiah 54:5), and “So I will betroth you to Me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion” (Hosea 2:19).

And the reign of God is the psalms' great cry: “The LORD reigns, let the earth rejoice” (Psalm 97:1).
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the Bible's story ends with a wedding, not an escape. Ask how the gift of the bride's clothing and her own righteous acts fit together in your life with God. And ask what good things you are tempted to give the worship that belongs to God alone.

passages.t: The rider on the white horse
passages.happening:
“Then I saw heaven standing open, and there before me was a white horse. And its rider is called Faithful and True. With righteousness He judges and wages war” (verse 11).

“He has eyes like blazing fire, and many royal crowns on His head. He has a name written on Him that only He Himself knows. He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, and His name is The Word of God” (verses 12-13).

“The armies of heaven, dressed in fine linen, white and pure, follow Him on white horses” (verse 14).

“And from His mouth proceeds a sharp sword with which to strike down the nations, and He will rule them with an iron scepter. He treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. And He has a name written on His robe and on His thigh: KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS” (verses 15-16).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the New Testament's great pictures of Christ, and nearly every detail says who he is.

Heaven stands open. In 4:1 a door opened in heaven for John to look in. Now heaven opens for Christ to come out.

His first name is ‘Faithful and True’. He is the one who keeps God's promises; he was called ‘the faithful and true Witness’ in 3:14. His eyes ‘like blazing fire’ are the eyes John saw in 1:14. He wears ‘many royal crowns’; the dragon and the beast wore crowns too, but his are the true ones. He has a name ‘that only He Himself knows’: he is never fully grasped by those who follow him.

His robe is ‘dipped in blood’ before any battle is told. Many interpreters take it as his own blood, since in Revelation the Lamb conquers by being slain (5:9; 12:11). Others read it from Isaiah 63, where the one who treads the winepress has garments stained with the blood of his enemies. These notes do not choose.

His name is ‘The Word of God’. That links Revelation to the opening of John's Gospel, where the Word was with God and was God and became flesh. And it explains how he fights. His sword comes ‘from His mouth’, not from his hand. He wins by speaking the truth. Isaiah said the promised king would ‘strike the earth with the rod of His mouth’.

‘The armies of heaven’ follow him, dressed in the same fine linen as the bride. They carry no weapons, and they do not fight. They ride behind him.

The first hearers knew what a victory procession looked like. When a Roman general won a great victory, the Senate might grant him a triumph, a procession through Rome in a chariot, by tradition drawn by white horses, with his army and his captives. Under the emperors that honour came to be kept for the emperor and his family. Coins, inscriptions and temples called the emperor lord and saviour. John sees a different victor. The name on his robe, ‘KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS’, is a direct answer to Caesar's claims.

The one who came the first time riding on a donkey, on the way to a cross, will come again as king and judge. The church confesses it in the Nicene Creed: he ‘shall come again, with glory, to judge both the quick and the dead’, the living and the dead.
passages.ot:
The sword of his mouth is Isaiah's promised king: “He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth and slay the wicked with the breath of His lips” (Isaiah 11:4).

The iron scepter is the king of Psalm 2: “You will break them with an iron scepter; You will shatter them like pottery” (Psalm 2:9).

The winepress is Isaiah's: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no one from the nations was with Me” (Isaiah 63:3).

And the humble king of the first coming is Zechariah's: “See, your King comes to you, righteous and victorious, humble and riding on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9).
passages.hard:
When does the rider come? Is this the second coming?

Christians read the scene in the four ways the book page sets out, and these notes do not choose. Preterists often see verses 11 to 21 as Christ's victory over the persecuting powers of the first century, some of them with a further look to the end. Historicists have placed it at various points in the church's history, usually near the end. Futurists see it as the visible return of Christ at the close of history to defeat a final world ruler, and premillennial futurists place it before the thousand years of chapter 20. Idealists read it as a picture of Christ's victory over evil, won at the cross, carried forward through the preaching of the gospel, and completed at his return.

Every Christian tradition confesses that Christ will return in glory. They differ on how much of this chapter describes that event directly. These notes set no date for it. Jesus said, “No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father” (Matthew 24:36).
passages.asks: Ask which of the rider's names you most need today: Faithful and True, The Word of God, or King of kings. Ask what it means that he conquers with the word of his mouth, and what that asks of those who follow him. And ask whether you look for his coming with longing, or with fear, and why.

passages.t: The beast and the false prophet taken
passages.happening:
“Then I saw an angel standing in the sun, and he cried out in a loud voice to all the birds flying overhead, ‘Come, gather together for the great supper of God, so that you may eat the flesh of kings and commanders and mighty men, of horses and riders, of everyone slave and free, small and great’” (verses 17-18).

“Then I saw the beast and the kings of the earth with their armies assembled to wage war against the One seated on the horse, and against His army” (verse 19).

“But the beast was captured along with the false prophet, who on its behalf had performed signs deceiving those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image. Both the beast and the false prophet were thrown alive into the fiery lake of burning sulfur” (verse 20).

“And the rest were killed with the sword that proceeded from the mouth of the One seated on the horse. And all the birds gorged themselves on their flesh” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
There are two suppers in this chapter, set side by side on purpose: ‘the marriage supper of the Lamb’ (verse 9) and ‘the great supper of God’ (verse 17). One is a wedding feast for the invited. The other is a terrible picture taken from Ezekiel, where birds are called to feed on the fallen army of Gog. The two suppers show the two ends of the book's story.

The enemies gather. The beast and the kings of the earth, gathered at the place called Armageddon in 16:16, now stand against the rider and his army. And then, remarkably, there is no battle. The next verse simply says the beast ‘was captured’. The fight is settled before it begins.

The beast and the false prophet, who rose in chapter 13, are thrown alive into ‘the fiery lake of burning sulfur’. The book is taking down its enemies in the reverse of the order in which they came: Babylon first (chapter 18), then the beast and the false prophet (here), then the dragon himself (chapter 20).

‘The rest were killed with the sword that proceeded from the mouth.’ Again the weapon is the sword from his mouth, his word. The scene is drawn from the prophets' judgment oracles, and its details show that it is not a cavalry battle to be pictured literally.

This is a hard passage, and it is meant to be. It is sober, and it is not to be enjoyed. It tells suffering churches that the powers which deceived the nations and killed God's people will not survive Christ's coming. It is not a call to Christians to fight. The armies of heaven in this chapter never strike a blow.
passages.ot:
The great supper is Ezekiel's: “Call out to every kind of bird and to every beast of the field: ‘Assemble and come together from all around to the sacrificial feast that I am preparing for you’” (Ezekiel 39:17).

The fire and sulfur go back to Sodom: “Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah” (Genesis 19:24).
passages.hard:
Does this bloody scene contradict the Jesus of the Gospels?

The violence of verses 17 to 21 troubles many readers, and the trouble is honest. Several things are worth weighing. The scene is built from Old Testament judgment oracles, Ezekiel 39, Isaiah 63 and Psalm 2, and its details show it is not a literal battle: the enemies are struck by a sword that comes from the rider's mouth, the power of his word. The battle is never fought; the enemies are simply captured. And the rider's robe is already bloody before any fighting, which fits the book's teaching that the Lamb won by his own death.

At the same time, the chapter does teach that Christ will judge, and so do the Gospels. Jesus said, “When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, He will sit on His glorious throne” (Matthew 25:31). The Jesus who wept over Jerusalem also warned of its judgment. Interpreters differ on how literally to take the scene. But the church across its history has held that the same Jesus who died for sinners will return to put an end to evil, and that his judgment is justice for the victims of the powers the beast stands for.

What the lake of fire is, and what it means for those thrown into it, is set out in the notes on chapter 20, where Christians' views are given without a side. These notes say nothing about the eternal state of any particular person. That belongs to God alone.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask which supper you are being invited to, and what it means that the invitation is still open. Ask what it means that the rider's army never fights, and what that says about how Christians resist evil. And ask whether you can trust the judge with the world's evil, because you know he died for sinners.
